group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 67-year-old man checked in this afternoon to the ambulatory peri-operative clinic five days ahead of a scheduled elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic biliary colic that has been disrupting sleep twice weekly; the general surgeon anticipates a single umbilical port plus two additional 5-mm ports, an operative duration of under one hour, minimal blood loss, and discharge later the same day if pain is controlled. The patient drove himself from a neighboring town, parked in the hospital garage, and walked the length of the skybridge to the clinic at an unhurried pace while carrying a small backpack; he reported mild shortness of breath when hurrying to keep an appointment but no chest pressure, arm discomfort, or palpitations. Home activities include mowing a modest lawn with a self-propelled mower, carrying groceries up a flight of stairs, and weekly nine-hole golf with a powered cart, all accomplished with only occasional fatigue. Approximately three years ago he was admitted for progressive dyspnea and bilateral ankle swelling; transthoracic echocardiography at that admission demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38 % with global hypokinesis, and intravenous diuretics produced a four-kilogram weight reduction over 48 hours. Since then, he has experienced one additional hospitalization last winter after dietary excess during the holidays; outpatient cardiology notes describe New York Heart Association class II symptoms that improve with strict salt restriction. His current regimen, taken as usual this morning, consists of carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg each morning, torsemide 20 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg nightly, and low-dose aspirin initiated by primary care for vascular protection; he keeps a daily weight log and calls if the scale creeps up by more than two pounds overnight. He denies ever having angina, myocardial infarction, coronary stenting, bypass surgery, or abnormal stress studies, and no prior electrocardiograms have revealed Q waves or significant ST-segment changes. Diabetes mellitus was diagnosed eight years ago after fasting glucose of 134 mg/dL; lifestyle modification and metformin 1000 mg twice daily have kept his most recent hemoglobin A1c at 6.9 % with fasting glucometer readings generally in the 110–130 mg/dL range, requiring no injectable therapy. Hypertension was recognized in midlife and is well controlled on the aforementioned agents; hyperlipidemia is managed with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He has never smoked, enjoys one glass of lager with weekend dinners, and denies recreational drug use. Surgical history includes an uncomplicated open appendectomy at age 20 and right cataract extraction at 64. Review of systems today is negative for paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthostatic dizziness, syncope, exertional claudication, fevers, weight loss, or gastrointestinal bleeding. After five minutes seated, vital signs are temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/76 mm Hg in the left arm, regular radial pulse 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air; he stands 174 cm tall, weighs 86 kg, and his body mass index is 28.4 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is estimated at 5 cm above the sternal angle, carotid pulses are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is palpated in the sixth interspace just lateral to the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft third heart sound and a grade 1/6 mid-peaking systolic murmur along the left sternal border without radiation; no friction rub is detected. Lung fields are clear centrally with faint bibasilar crackles that resolve after several deep breaths. The abdomen is soft, non-distended, and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant without guarding or rebound; Murphy sign is negative today, and no hepatosplenomegaly is appreciated. Extremities are warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and trace pitting edema at both ankles. A focused neurologic screen shows intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength, normal sensation, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before the visit reveal hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, white blood cell count 6.5 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 226 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.29 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 58 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose in the same sample is 122 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows sinus rhythm at 72 beats per minute, normal PR interval, narrow QRS complexes, and nonspecific T-wave flattening unchanged from a tracing six months earlier. Upright chest radiography demonstrates a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette with clear lungs and no pleural effusion. Airway assessment by anesthesia records a Mallampati class II view, 4 cm inter-incisor distance, full cervical extension, and good mandibular protrusion. The anesthesiologist plans standard induction with endotracheal intubation, continuation of the beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor on the morning of surgery, withholding the loop diuretic that day to avoid intravascular depletion, hourly blood glucose checks, and goal-directed fluid therapy guided by non-invasive cardiac output monitoring. Sequential compression devices, early ambulation, and incentive spirometry have been prescribed post-operatively, and the patient has been instructed to remain nil per os after midnight except for clear liquids up to two hours before hospital arrival. After discussing potential complications—bleeding, bile leak, conversion to open procedure, pulmonary or cardiac decompensation—he voiced understanding, signed the necessary consent documents, and expressed readiness to proceed with the planned cholecystectomy.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns one point per risk factor. The result hinges on how the operation is classified:
- History of heart failure: prior admissions for congestion, EF 38%, and NYHA class II symptoms → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: no documented MI, angina, positive stress test, or pathologic Q waves → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no documented stroke or TIA → 0.
- Preoperative insulin use: diabetes is treated with metformin alone → 0.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine is 1.29 mg/dL → 0.
- High-risk surgery: the original RCRI includes intraperitoneal procedures, so laparoscopic cholecystectomy adds 1 under that definition, giving 2. A total of 1 assumes the elective laparoscopic procedure is not counted as high-risk.
With that procedural assumption: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
